definition: The rate at which charge passes a point, measured in amperes.
wrongs: The energy per unit charge between two points.
The opposition of a resistor to charge flow.
The reciprocal of resistance.
why: One ampere is one coulomb of charge passing a point each second.
example: A lamp filament carries a steady flow of charge equal to two coulombs every second.
scenario: A charge of 6 coulombs passes a point in 2 seconds. State the current in amperes.
scenarioWhy: Current is charge divided by time, so 6 coulombs in 2 seconds is 3 amperes.

definition: The energy per unit charge required to move charge between two points, measured in volts.
wrongs: The rate at which charge passes a point.
The product of resistance and conductance.
The reciprocal of current.
why: One volt is one joule of energy given to each coulomb moved between the two points.
example: A battery supplies four joules for every coulomb that leaves its positive terminal and returns to the negative.
scenario: Moving 3 coulombs through an element requires 12 joules. State the voltage in volts.
scenarioWhy: Voltage is energy divided by charge, so 12 joules for 3 coulombs is 4 volts.

definition: The opposition of an element to current, equal to voltage divided by current for an ohmic element.
wrongs: The rate of charge flow through an element.
The energy stored in a magnetic field.
The reciprocal of voltage.
why: Ohmic materials have a constant ratio of voltage to current, and that ratio is the resistance.
example: A heater draws 2 amperes when 10 volts is placed across its terminals.
scenario: An element has 10 volts across it and 2 amperes through it. State its resistance in ohms.
scenarioWhy: Resistance is voltage divided by current, so 10 volts divided by 2 amperes is 5 ohms.

definition: The relation that the voltage across a resistor equals the current through it multiplied by its resistance.
wrongs: The rule that the sum of currents at a node is zero.
The rule that the sum of voltages around a loop is zero.
The rule that a resistive load should equal the source resistance for maximum power.
why: For a resistor, V, I, and R are tied by V = IR at every instant in the lumped model.
example: A 4 ohm heater carrying 3 amperes must have 12 volts across its terminals.
scenario: A 4 ohm resistor carries 3 amperes. State the voltage across it in volts.
scenarioWhy: Ohm's law gives voltage as 4 ohms times 3 amperes, which is 12 volts.

definition: The rate of energy transfer in an element, equal to the product of its voltage and current.
wrongs: The energy stored per coulomb.
The opposition to current.
The sum of voltages around a loop.
why: Multiplying volts by amperes yields joules per second, which is watts.
example: A phone charger delivers 5 volts at 2 amperes to a handset.
scenario: A device draws 2 amperes from a 5 volt source. State the power absorbed in watts.
scenarioWhy: Power is voltage times current, so 5 volts times 2 amperes is 10 watts.

definition: The principle that the algebraic sum of the currents leaving a node is zero.
wrongs: The principle that the algebraic sum of voltages around a loop is zero.
The relation that voltage equals current times resistance.
The rule that parallel resistors share one current.
why: Charge does not accumulate at a node in the lumped-circuit model, so currents in must balance currents out.
example: At a junction, 4 amperes and 5 amperes arrive on two wires, and one wire carries the total away.
scenario: Currents of 4 amperes and 5 amperes enter a node, and one current leaves. State the leaving current in amperes.
scenarioWhy: The current law requires the single leaving current to equal 4 amperes plus 5 amperes.

definition: The principle that the algebraic sum of the voltages around a closed loop is zero.
wrongs: The principle that the algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero.
The rule that parallel elements have different voltages.
The formula for capacitive reactance.
why: Energy conservation around a closed path requires the voltage rises and drops to balance.
example: A loop contains a battery and two resistors, and the two resistor voltages add up to the battery voltage.
scenario: Two series resistors drop 7 volts and 8 volts. State the source voltage, in volts, that closes the loop.
scenarioWhy: Around the loop, the source voltage must equal the sum of the drops, 7 volts plus 8 volts.

definition: A connection in which elements carry the same current and their voltages add.
wrongs: A connection in which elements have the same voltage and their currents add.
A connection that forces the voltage between two nodes to zero.
A connection that leaves a branch current at zero by a break.
why: There is only one path, so the same current passes through each series element.
example: Two lamp filaments are placed one after another on a single path, so the same current heats both.
scenario: Resistors of 3 ohms and 7 ohms lie on one path and carry the same current. State their equivalent resistance in ohms.
scenarioWhy: Resistances on one current path add, so 3 ohms plus 7 ohms is 10 ohms.

definition: A connection in which elements have the same voltage and their currents add.
wrongs: A connection in which elements carry the same current and their voltages add.
A connection used only for magnetic coupling.
A connection that stores charge on two plates.
why: Parallel elements share both end nodes, so each has the same terminal voltage.
example: Two identical lamps are tied across the same battery, and each lamp sees the full battery voltage.
scenario: Two resistors of 6 ohms are tied across the same two nodes. State the equivalent resistance in ohms.
scenarioWhy: Two equal resistances in parallel have an equivalent of half of one of them, so 6 ohms becomes 3 ohms.

definition: A series string of resistors that splits a source voltage in proportion to the resistances.
wrongs: A parallel pair that splits a source current.
A transformer that isolates two grounds.
An inductor that blocks DC.
why: The same series current times each resistance gives a drop proportional to that resistance.
example: A 12 volt battery feeds 2 ohms in series with 4 ohms, and the larger resistor drops more of the 12 volts.
scenario: A 12 volt source feeds 2 ohms in series with 4 ohms. State the voltage across the 4 ohm resistor in volts.
scenarioWhy: The 4 ohm resistor takes 4/6 of 12 volts, which is 8 volts.

definition: A parallel pair of resistors that splits a source current so each branch current is inversely related to its resistance.
wrongs: A series string that splits a source voltage.
A diode bridge that reverses half of an AC wave.
A capacitor that blocks DC current.
why: The smaller parallel resistor has the larger conductance and therefore carries more of the source current.
example: A 5 ampere source feeds 10 ohms in parallel with 15 ohms, and the 10 ohm branch carries the larger share.
scenario: A 5 ampere source feeds 10 ohms in parallel with 15 ohms. State the current in the 10 ohm branch, in amperes.
scenarioWhy: The 10 ohm branch carries 5 amperes times 15/25, which is 3 amperes.

definition: A point in a circuit where two or more elements are joined together.
wrongs: A loop that contains no other loop.
A device that stores charge.
A source whose value depends on another current.
why: Joined terminals are at one voltage, and the current law is written at that point.
example: Three resistor leads are soldered to one pad, and that pad is treated as a single voltage point.
scenario: Three resistor leads meet at one solder pad that has a single voltage. Name that connection point.
scenarioWrongs: A loop with no inner loop
scenarioWhy: A point where element terminals join is a node.

definition: A loop in a planar circuit that does not contain any other loop inside it.
wrongs: A point where several elements join.
An open branch with zero current.
A phasor ratio of voltage to current.
why: Mesh analysis assigns one current to each such empty loop and writes the voltage law there.
example: A window-shaped circuit has two inner openings, and each opening is traced as its own current loop.
scenario: A planar circuit is divided into loops that contain no smaller loop. Name one of those empty loops.
scenarioWrongs: A ratio of voltage to current
scenarioWhy: A loop that encloses no other loop is a mesh.

definition: A solution method that uses node voltages as unknowns and writes the current law at the essential nodes.
wrongs: A method that uses mesh currents and the voltage law.
A method that activates one independent source at a time.
A method that replaces a network by a current source in parallel with a resistance.
why: After a reference node is chosen, each other node voltage is found from the current law.
example: A student labels two unknown voltages relative to ground and writes one current-balance equation at each of those nodes.
scenario: Unknowns are voltages measured from a reference node, and the current law is written at each of those nodes. Name that method.
scenarioWrongs: Activating one source at a time
Replacing the network by a parallel current source
scenarioWhy: Using node voltages and the current law is nodal analysis.

definition: A solution method that uses mesh currents as unknowns and writes the voltage law around each mesh.
wrongs: A method that uses node voltages and the current law.
A method that open-circuits a load to find a voltage.
A method that adds responses of independent sources.
why: Each mesh current circulates around one empty loop, and the voltage law supplies one equation per mesh.
example: A student assigns clockwise currents to two window loops and writes a voltage sum around each window.
scenario: Unknowns are currents circulating around empty loops, and the voltage law is written on each loop. Name that method.
scenarioWhy: Using mesh currents and the voltage law is mesh analysis.

definition: The single resistance that draws the same current from a source as the original resistor network.
wrongs: The open-circuit voltage of a network.
The short-circuit current of a network.
The time constant of a capacitor circuit.
why: At the source terminals, one resistor can replace the network if it has the same terminal V-I behavior.
example: Three 5 ohm resistors in a single path are replaced by one resistor before the source current is computed.
scenario: Three resistors of 5 ohms each lie in series. State the single equivalent resistance in ohms.
scenarioWhy: Series resistances add, so three 5 ohm resistors equal 15 ohms.

definition: A two-terminal model of a linear network made of one voltage source in series with one resistance.
wrongs: A model made of one current source in parallel with one resistance.
A model made of only an ideal wire.
A model made of a capacitor in series with an inductor.
why: The series voltage is the open-circuit voltage, and the series resistance is found with independent sources deactivated.
example: A bias network seen by a load is redrawn as 10 volts in series with 5 ohms.
scenario: A linear network seen by a load is redrawn as one voltage source in series with one resistance. Name that model.
scenarioWhy: One voltage source in series with one resistance is the Thevenin model.

definition: A two-terminal model of a linear network made of one current source in parallel with one resistance.
wrongs: A model made of one voltage source in series with one resistance.
A model that keeps every original source in place.
A model used only for nonlinear diodes.
why: The parallel current is the short-circuit current, and the parallel resistance equals the Thevenin resistance.
example: The same bias network is redrawn as 2 amperes in parallel with 5 ohms before a load is attached.
scenario: A linear network is redrawn as one current source in parallel with one resistance. Name that model.
scenarioWhy: One current source in parallel with one resistance is the Norton model.

definition: A method for linear circuits that finds each independent source's response alone and adds those responses.
wrongs: A method that replaces a network by one voltage source and one resistance.
A method that sets the load equal to the source resistance.
A method that writes only mesh equations.
why: Linearity lets responses add, while dependent sources stay active and are never turned off.
example: A circuit has a battery and a current source, so the resistor voltage is computed twice, once for each source, and then added.
scenario: A linear circuit has two independent sources. Each is activated alone, with the other deactivated, and the voltages are added. Name that method.
scenarioWrongs: Replacing the network by a series voltage source
Matching the load to the source resistance
scenarioWhy: Finding each independent source's response and adding them is superposition.

definition: Replacing a voltage source in series with a resistance by a current source of V/R in parallel with that resistance, or the reverse.
wrongs: Turning off every source to find a time constant.
Replacing a diode by an open circuit in both directions.
Splitting one resistor into two series parts with no change of source type.
why: Both forms produce the same voltage and current at the external terminals.
example: A 12 volt source in series with 4 ohms is redrawn as a current source in parallel with 4 ohms.
scenario: A 12 volt source in series with 4 ohms becomes a current source in parallel with 4 ohms. State that current in amperes.
scenarioWhy: The equivalent current is 12 volts divided by 4 ohms, which is 3 amperes.

definition: The resistive-load condition in which the load equals the resistance seen looking back into the network.
wrongs: The condition that the load is zero so current is largest.
The condition that the load is infinite so voltage is largest.
The condition that the load is half the source voltage.
why: For a Thevenin resistance Rth, power in a resistive load peaks when the load equals Rth.
example: A sensor is modeled as a source with 8 ohms of internal resistance, and the attached resistive load is also 8 ohms.
scenario: The resistance seen by a resistive load is 8 ohms. State the load, in ohms, that absorbs maximum power.
scenarioWhy: Maximum power occurs when the resistive load equals the 8 ohm resistance of the source network.

definition: A voltage or current source whose value does not depend on any other voltage or current in the circuit.
wrongs: A source whose value is a constant times some other voltage or current.
A resistor whose voltage depends on its current.
A capacitor whose current depends on voltage slope.
why: A battery or a fixed current source keeps its specified value regardless of the rest of the circuit, within its ratings.
example: A laboratory supply is set to 5 volts and holds that voltage whether the attached resistor is 100 ohms or 200 ohms.
scenario: A supply is set to 5 volts and does not change that setting when the load resistor changes. Which source type is it?
scenarioAnswer: A source with its own fixed value
scenarioWrongs: A source set by another circuit variable
scenarioWhy: A source whose value is set by itself, not by another circuit variable, is independent.

definition: A voltage or current source whose value is controlled by a voltage or current elsewhere in the circuit.
wrongs: A source whose value is fixed by the user and by nothing in the circuit.
An ideal wire between two nodes.
A resistor that only converts energy to heat.
why: The controlling variable may be a branch current or a node-pair voltage, and the source scales that variable.
example: A diamond-shaped source outputs a current equal to three times the current through a distant resistor.
scenario: A current source outputs three times the current measured in another branch. Which source type is it?
scenarioAnswer: A source controlled by another variable
scenarioWrongs: A source with a fixed user setting
scenarioWhy: A source set by a current elsewhere in the circuit is dependent.

definition: A break that forces the current in that branch to zero.
wrongs: An ideal wire that forces the voltage between two points to zero.
A capacitor in sinusoidal steady state.
A resistor equal to the Thevenin resistance.
why: With the path broken, no charge flows, while the voltage across the break may be nonzero.
example: A switch in a lamp branch is opened, and the lamp current falls to zero while voltage remains across the switch.
scenario: A switch opens and the current in that lamp branch becomes zero. Name that branch condition.
scenarioWhy: A break that forces branch current to zero is an open circuit.

definition: An ideal connection that forces the voltage between two points to zero.
wrongs: A break that forces a branch current to zero.
An infinite resistance.
A resonant circuit with zero reactance only at one frequency.
why: An ideal wire has zero resistance, so the voltage law leaves no drop between its ends.
example: A screwdriver accidentally joins the two terminals of a battery, and the voltage between those terminals collapses.
scenario: An ideal wire joins two nodes so the voltage between them is zero. Name that connection.
scenarioWhy: An ideal connection with zero voltage between its ends is a short circuit.

definition: An element that stores energy in an electric field and whose current equals C times the derivative of voltage.
wrongs: An element whose voltage equals L times the derivative of current.
An element whose voltage equals current times a constant resistance.
A source whose value is fixed by the user.
why: Current through a capacitor is proportional to how fast its voltage is changing, not to the voltage itself.
example: When the voltage on a timing element is constant, that element draws no current even though voltage remains across it.
scenario: Long after a DC source is applied, the current in an ideal capacitor is zero. How does that capacitor behave?
scenarioWhy: Zero current with a possible nonzero voltage is the open-circuit behavior of a capacitor in DC steady state.

definition: An element that stores energy in a magnetic field and whose voltage equals L times the derivative of current.
wrongs: An element whose current equals C times the derivative of voltage.
An element that dissipates energy as heat in proportion to current squared.
A diode that conducts in only one direction.
why: Voltage across an inductor is proportional to how fast its current is changing.
example: A coil on a relay holds a steady current and the voltage measured across that coil is then zero.
scenario: Long after a DC source is applied, the voltage across an ideal inductor is zero. How does that inductor behave?
scenarioWhy: Zero voltage while current may be nonzero is the short-circuit behavior of an inductor in DC steady state.

definition: The product of resistance and capacitance that sets the speed of a first-order resistor-capacitor response.
wrongs: The ratio of inductance to resistance.
The product of inductance and capacitance.
The sum of resistance and capacitance.
why: The source-free capacitor voltage changes with the exponential rate 1 over RC.
example: A timer uses 4 ohms in series with 2 farads, and the exponential is written with an 8 second scale.
scenario: A series RC circuit has R equal to 4 ohms and C equal to 2 farads. State the time constant in seconds.
scenarioWhy: The RC time constant is R times C, so 4 times 2 is 8 seconds.

definition: The ratio of inductance to resistance that sets the speed of a first-order resistor-inductor response.
wrongs: The product of resistance and capacitance.
The product of resistance and inductance.
The difference of inductance and resistance.
why: The source-free inductor current changes with the exponential rate R over L.
example: A coil of 8 henries is discharged through 2 ohms, and the current decays on a 4 second scale.
scenario: A series RL circuit has L equal to 8 henries and R equal to 2 ohms. State the time constant in seconds.
scenarioWhy: The RL time constant is L divided by R, so 8 henries divided by 2 ohms is 4 seconds.

definition: The source-free part of a circuit's behavior, set by stored energy and typically an exponential decay.
wrongs: The particular response that remains after a long-lived DC source has settled the circuit.
The sinusoidal steady state at resonance.
The response of an ideal diode in breakdown.
why: With independent sources removed, only the energy already stored in capacitors or inductors drives the transient.
example: After a switch removes a battery, a capacitor voltage falls exponentially through the remaining resistor.
scenario: A switch removes the battery, and a capacitor voltage then decays exponentially through a resistor. Name that source-free behavior.
scenarioWrongs: The settled response to a lasting DC source
scenarioWhy: An exponential decay after the source is removed is the natural response.

definition: The settled condition, long after constant sources are applied, when capacitor currents and inductor voltages are zero.
wrongs: The instant just after a switch changes, when stored variables have not yet moved.
The source-free exponential that dies away.
The frequency at which reactances cancel.
why: Constant voltages and currents have zero derivatives, so a capacitor acts open and an inductor acts short.
example: Minutes after a DC supply is connected, a coupling capacitor carries no current and a series coil drops no voltage.
scenario: Long after constant sources are applied, derivatives have died and stored-element derivatives are zero. Name that condition.
scenarioWhy: The settled condition under constant sources, with zero capacitor current and zero inductor voltage, is DC steady state.

definition: The equivalent DC value of a periodic waveform that delivers the same average power to a resistor.
wrongs: The peak value of a sine wave.
The peak-to-peak value of a sine wave.
The average of a sine wave over a whole number of cycles, which is zero.
why: For a sine wave, that equivalent is the peak divided by the square root of 2.
example: A wall outlet sine wave with a peak of about 170 volts has an effective value near 120 volts.
scenario: A sine wave has a peak of 10 volts. State its RMS value in volts, rounded to two decimal places.
scenarioWhy: The RMS value of a sine wave is the peak divided by the square root of 2, and 10 divided by that factor is 7.07.

definition: A complex number that represents the amplitude and phase of a sinusoid at one fixed frequency.
wrongs: The instantaneous waveform written as a function of time.
A DC offset added to a sine wave.
The time constant of a transient.
why: Suppressing the common rotating time factor lets AC circuits be solved with complex algebra.
example: A cosine of amplitude 6 and phase 30 degrees is written as the complex value 6 at angle 30 degrees.
scenario: A cosine of amplitude 6 and phase 30 degrees is replaced by a complex amplitude for AC analysis. Name that complex representation.
scenarioWhy: A complex number holding amplitude and phase of a fixed-frequency sinusoid is a phasor.

definition: The complex ratio of a voltage phasor to the current phasor at the same frequency, in ohms.
wrongs: The reciprocal of that complex ratio.
A purely real resistance with no phase shift.
The average power divided by the RMS current.
why: Impedance generalizes resistance to inductors and capacitors by using phasors, so it may be complex.
example: A coil's voltage phasor leads its current phasor by 90 degrees, and their ratio is a positive imaginary number.
scenario: In the phasor domain, a voltage complex value is divided by the current complex value at the same frequency. Name that ratio.
scenarioWrongs: A resistance that cannot have phase
scenarioWhy: The complex ratio of voltage phasor to current phasor is impedance.

definition: The magnitude of a capacitor's opposition to sinusoidal current, equal to 1 divided by omega C.
wrongs: The quantity omega times L.
The resistance of a carbon resistor.
The conductance of a parallel branch.
why: A capacitor passes high-frequency current more easily, so this opposition falls as frequency rises.
example: At 2 radians per second, a 1 farad capacitor opposes sinusoidal current by half an ohm.
scenario: A capacitor of 1 farad operates at 2 radians per second. State its reactance magnitude in ohms.
scenarioWhy: Capacitive reactance is 1 divided by omega C, so 1 divided by 2 is 0.5 ohms.

definition: The magnitude of an inductor's opposition to sinusoidal current, equal to omega times L.
wrongs: The quantity 1 divided by omega C.
The DC resistance of the coil wire only.
The resonant frequency in hertz.
why: An inductor opposes fast changes of current, so this opposition rises as frequency rises.
example: A 3 henry coil at 4 radians per second opposes sinusoidal current by 12 ohms.
scenario: An inductor of 3 henries operates at 4 radians per second. State its reactance magnitude in ohms.
scenarioWhy: Inductive reactance is omega times L, so 4 times 3 is 12 ohms.

definition: The AC condition in an RLC circuit at which the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel.
wrongs: The DC condition in which a capacitor is an open circuit.
The instant after a switch closes.
The bias region in which a diode is off.
why: When the reactances are equal, a series RLC circuit has minimum impedance and a purely resistive current.
example: A series RLC tuner is adjusted until the coil's reactance equals the capacitor's reactance and the source current peaks.
scenario: A series RLC circuit is at resonance and the inductive reactance is 20 ohms. State the capacitive reactance in ohms.
scenarioWhy: At series resonance the two reactances are equal, so the capacitive reactance is also 20 ohms.

definition: The cosine of the phase angle between voltage and current, equal to real power divided by apparent power.
wrongs: The sine of the phase angle between voltage and current.
The product of RMS voltage and RMS current with no angle.
The difference between inductive and capacitive reactance.
why: Only the in-phase component of current contributes to average power, and that fraction is the cosine of the angle.
example: A heater draws current in phase with its voltage, so all of its apparent power is real power.
scenario: Voltage and current of a load are in phase. State the power factor.
scenarioWhy: The phase angle is zero, and the cosine of zero is 1, so the power factor is unity.

definition: A diode model that is a short circuit when forward biased and an open circuit when reverse biased.
wrongs: A diode model with a constant 0.7 volt drop whenever it conducts.
A diode model that conducts equally in both directions.
A diode model that is always an open circuit.
why: The ideal model keeps zero drop while conducting and zero current while blocking.
example: In a first-pass rectifier sketch, the conducting device is replaced by a wire and the blocking device by a gap.
scenario: An ideal diode is forward biased and conducting. Which simple element replaces it?
scenarioWhy: A forward-biased ideal diode has zero voltage drop, so it is replaced by a short circuit.

definition: The diode bias in which the anode is at a higher potential than the cathode, allowing conduction.
wrongs: The bias in which the cathode is higher than the anode and an ideal diode is off.
The reverse-breakdown region used by a regulator diode.
The zero-voltage condition with no applied source.
why: That polarity reduces the junction barrier so carriers can cross and current rises quickly.
example: A silicon rectifier has its anode tied to the positive side of a DC source and its cathode toward the load return.
scenario: A diode anode is more positive than its cathode, and the diode conducts. Name that bias.
scenarioWhy: A higher anode potential that turns the diode on is forward bias.

definition: The diode bias in which the cathode is at a higher potential than the anode, so an ideal diode blocks.
wrongs: The bias in which the anode is higher and the diode conducts.
The intended breakdown region of a regulator diode.
The active region of a bipolar transistor.
why: That polarity widens the junction barrier, and only a tiny leakage flows in an ordinary diode.
example: A protection diode has its cathode held positive relative to its anode so it stays off during normal operation.
scenario: A diode cathode is more positive than its anode, and an ideal diode carries no current. Name that bias.
scenarioWhy: A higher cathode potential that keeps an ideal diode off is reverse bias.

definition: A diode designed to operate in reverse breakdown at a specified voltage and used to hold that voltage.
wrongs: A diode that emits light when forward biased.
A diode that generates current from incident light.
A diode chosen for a very small forward drop from a metal-semiconductor junction.
why: In breakdown, the voltage stays near the rated value over a useful range of reverse current.
example: A regulator diode holds a 5.1 volt rail while the reverse current varies within its rated range.
scenario: A diode is intended to hold a nearly constant voltage while operating in reverse breakdown. Which diode is that?
scenarioWhy: A diode used in controlled reverse breakdown to hold a voltage is a Zener diode.

definition: An op-amp model with infinite open-loop gain, infinite input impedance, and zero output impedance.
wrongs: An op-amp model with zero open-loop gain.
An op-amp model that draws large input current.
An op-amp model whose output resistance is infinite.
why: Infinite gain with negative feedback forces the input difference toward zero, and infinite input impedance draws no input current.
example: In a first analysis, both input terminals of a feedback amplifier are assumed to draw no current at all.
scenario: State the current, in amperes, drawn by either input terminal of an ideal op-amp.
scenarioWhy: Infinite input impedance means an ideal op-amp input current is zero.

definition: An op-amp connection whose closed-loop gain is the negative ratio of the feedback resistor to the input resistor.
wrongs: A connection whose gain is one plus a resistor ratio and whose input is on the plus terminal.
A connection whose gain is exactly one.
A connection with no feedback resistor.
why: The input is applied through a resistor to the inverting terminal, so the output has the opposite sign.
example: With 20 kilohms of feedback and 10 kilohms at the input, a 1 volt input becomes a negative 2 volt output.
scenario: Feedback is 20 kilohms and the input resistor is 10 kilohms in an inverting op-amp. State the closed-loop voltage gain.
scenarioWhy: The inverting gain is the negative of 20 kilohms divided by 10 kilohms, which is -2.

definition: An op-amp connection whose closed-loop gain is one plus the ratio of the feedback resistor to the grounded resistor.
wrongs: A connection whose gain is the negative of a resistor ratio.
A connection whose gain is exactly zero.
A connection that uses positive feedback to latch.
why: The signal enters the plus terminal, and the divider from output to the minus terminal sets a positive gain of at least one.
example: Feedback of 9 kilohms to a 1 kilohm grounded resistor gives a gain of ten for a signal on the plus terminal.
scenario: Feedback is 9 kilohms and the resistor from the inverting input to ground is 1 kilohm. State the non-inverting closed-loop gain.
scenarioWhy: The gain is 1 plus 9 kilohms divided by 1 kilohm, which is 10.

definition: An op-amp connection that ties the output to the inverting input and produces a voltage gain of one.
wrongs: A connection with a large negative gain.
A summing connection with several inputs.
An open-loop comparator with no feedback.
why: Unity feedback forces the output to copy the voltage applied to the non-inverting input while drawing no input current.
example: A sensor that cannot supply current drives the plus terminal, and the op-amp output, tied back to the minus terminal, drives the next stage.
scenario: The output is tied directly to the inverting input, and the signal enters the non-inverting input. State the voltage gain.
scenarioWhy: Direct feedback from the output to the inverting input makes the gain equal to 1.

definition: The ideal-op-amp result, under negative feedback, that the two input terminals are at the same voltage.
wrongs: A real wire soldered between the two input pins.
Saturation of the output at a supply rail.
Positive feedback that latches the output.
why: Infinite open-loop gain cannot have a finite output unless the differential input voltage is zero.
example: With negative feedback, a designer sets the inverting-input voltage equal to the non-inverting-input voltage before writing the resistor equations.
scenario: Negative feedback and infinite gain force the two op-amp input terminals to one voltage, without a wire between them. Name that condition.
scenarioWhy: Equal input voltages caused by negative feedback, without a physical short, is the virtual short.

definition: An inverting op-amp connection whose output is a weighted negative sum of two or more input voltages.
wrongs: A follower that copies one input.
A difference amplifier with exactly one output equal to one input.
A comparator that only reports which input is larger.
why: Each input current is a voltage over its resistor, and those currents sum through the feedback resistor.
example: Two equal input resistors and an equal feedback resistor turn input voltages of 2 volts and 5 volts into an output of negative 7 volts.
scenario: An inverting summer uses equal resistors on two inputs and on the feedback path. The inputs are 2 volts and 5 volts. State the output in volts.
scenarioWhy: With equal resistors, the output is the negative of 2 volts plus 5 volts, which is -7 volts.

definition: The rule that power absorbed is voltage times current when current enters the positive-labeled voltage terminal.

why: With that current direction, a positive product means the element absorbs power, and a negative product means it supplies power.

definition: The reciprocal of resistance, measured in siemens, which adds for elements connected in parallel.
wrongs: The product of voltage and current.

why: A larger conductance draws more current at the same voltage, and parallel paths add their conductances.
